extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students and instructors (introductory proof-writing / discrete math)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for learning to read, write, and evaluate rigorous undergraduate mathematical proofs (techniques, notation, and mathematical writing). Suitable for a semester-long 'introduction to proofs' course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters 4 through 6 are concerned with three main techniques used for proving theorems that have the “conditional” form “If P, then Q.” Chapter 4: Direct Proof (4.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach conditional statements by assuming the hypothesis P and deducing Q using definitions and elementary reasoning. Use cases when appropriate (see 'Using Cases' and 'Treating Similar Cases'). Presented as the primary technique for straightforward 'If P then Q' proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive Proof
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove 'If P then Q', prove the logically equivalent contrapositive 'If not Q then not P.' Useful when the contrapositive is more directly accessible than the forward implication. Pay attention to correct handling of negations and quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by Contradiction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the statement to be false (or assume both a hypothesis and the negation of the desired conclusion) and derive a contradiction. Use when direct approaches are awkward; be explicit about the assumption you negate and the contradiction obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by Cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Using Cases (Chapter 4.4) and Treating Similar Cases (4.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split the hypothesis into exhaustive, mutually exclusive cases and prove the conclusion in each case. When several cases are essentially identical, group them or treat them together to avoid repetition (see 'treating similar cases'). Clearly indicate the partition of cases and why they cover all possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Induction and Variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical Induction (Chapter 10) including proof by induction (10.1), strong induction (10.2), and proof by smallest counterexample (10.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For statements indexed by the naturals, provide a clear basis (base case) and inductive step (show n to n+1). For strong induction, assume the statement for all smaller indices to prove n. For smallest-counterexample proofs, assume a minimal counterexample and derive a contradiction. Be explicit about the induction hypothesis and the domain of the index.

rubrics_metrics.name: If-and-Only-If (Bi-conditional) Proofs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove both directions separately: 'If P then Q' and 'If Q then P.' Alternatively, show equivalence via a chain of logically equivalent statements. Explicitly label which direction you are proving to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and Uniqueness Proofs (constructive vs non-constructive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence Proofs; Existence and Uniqueness Proofs (Chapter 7.3–7.4) and the distinction 'Constructive Versus Non-Constructive Proofs'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For existence: either construct an example explicitly (constructive proof) or show existence indirectly (non-constructive). For uniqueness: assume two objects satisfy the specification and show they must be equal. When possible, provide a constructive witness; if using a non-constructive argument, clearly justify why existence follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof via Counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: Disproof (Chapter 9) with Counterexamples (9.1) and Disproving Existence Statements (9.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To disprove a universal statement, give a specific counterexample that violates it. To disprove an existence claim, show that no object can satisfy the required properties (often by contradiction). When giving a counterexample, verify it satisfies the hypothesis but not the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial (Counting) Proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorial Proof (Chapter 3.10 and Chapter 3 generally on counting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinatorial interpretations (counting arguments, bijections, inclusion–exclusion, pigeonhole principle) to establish equalities or inequalities. Be explicit about the objects being counted and justify counting steps (e.g., multiplication/addition principles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Definitions and Explicit Assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The book emphasizes laying out definitions (e.g., definition of set, ordered pair, Cartesian product) and using them in proofs (multiple instances throughout Chapters 1–14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and use precise definitions; when a proof uses a definition, indicate which part of the definition is applied. Make hypotheses explicit at the start of proofs so readers know what is assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Structure and Quantifier Handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections on Quantifiers (2.8), Negating Statements (2.10), and Logical Inference (2.11) stress correct logical manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay careful attention to the order and scope of quantifiers (for all, there exists) and their negations. When negating complex statements, apply De Morgan’s laws and move negation across quantifiers correctly. Use truth-table reasoning or symbolic manipulation where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Writing and Notation Precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Several explicit style and notation cautions appear (e.g., 'Be careful in writing the empty set. Don’t write {Ø} when you mean Ø.'; choices about set-builder punctuation: 'We use the colon.'). There is a chapter/section titled 'Mathematical Writing' (5.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard, unambiguous notation consistently. Avoid common notational confusions (empty set vs set containing empty set, bars for absolute value vs cardinality). State the conventions you adopt when necessary (e.g., using ':' in set-builder notation). Strive for clear sentence structure and readable proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity about Parentheses and Grouping in Expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of parentheses. The text warns about distinctions such as R x (N x Z) (ordered pairs with second entry an ordered pair) versus R x N x Z (ordered triples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming Cartesian products or nested structures, be explicit about grouping and the type of ordered object you mean. If you blur the distinction, annotate it or explain why the distinction is irrelevant in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct Use of Examples, Diagrams, and Pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: The text uses diagrams to explain Cartesian products and Venn/graph illustrations (Figures 1.1–1.4) and notes that subsets and functions are often easier to understand visually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams to illustrate constructions or counterexamples, but accompany pictures with precise symbolic description. Ensure any visual argument is backed by a rigorous explanation when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of Mathematical Documents (Theorem/Proof/Lemma/Corollary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book regularly organizes material into theorems, definitions, examples, facts, and exercises (e.g., Definition 1.2, Fact 1.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present results with a clear label (Theorem, Proposition, Lemma, Fact), followed by a proof. Use corollaries and remarks appropriately. Keep proofs self-contained: state what's being assumed and what is being proved at the outset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Level of Rigor for Audience and Context
rubrics_metrics.description: The Preface and Introduction explain the book is for students transitioning from computational to theoretical mathematics, stressing proof techniques and conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match rigor to the course aims: be rigorous enough to justify each step but avoid unnecessary pedantry. Indicate when heuristic or intuitive arguments are being given versus formal proofs. For assignments/exams, follow instructor-prescribed rigor levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful Distinction Between Similar Mathematical Objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The text repeatedly stresses distinctions such as an element vs subset (e.g., {1,3} ∈ B vs {1,3} ⊆ B), matrices vs 6-tuples (M ≠ R^6 even if similar), and sequences vs sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly indicate whether an object is being treated as an element, a subset, an ordered tuple, or another structure. Avoid conflating objects that are mathematically different even if they have similar representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit Domain/Codomain and Function Properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 12 covers functions, injective and surjective functions, composition and inverse functions, image and preimage; solutions later stress giving domain and codomain when discussing bijections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving statements about functions, explicitly state domain and codomain. To prove injectivity/surjectivity, use the standard definitions and show the appropriate quantifier-based conditions. When constructing bijections for cardinality arguments, give the explicit mapping and prove injective/surjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Established Facts and Dependency Awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: The book provides a dependency tree for chapters and notes which results are prerequisites (e.g., Chapters 1–3 underpin later chapters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing proofs, cite prior facts or theorems you depend on and ensure prerequisites are satisfied. For longer arguments, break into lemmas and reference them to clarify dependencies.
